o: We must decide whether `nums` is the **unique** shortest supersequence of all given subsequences. A shortest supersequence is essentially a topological ordering of a DAG built from ordering constraints: every consecutive pair `(a, b)` in any sequence forces `a` to appear before `b`. The supersequence is unique exactly when at every step of Kahn's algorithm there is **exactly one** node with in-degree 0 — if two nodes are simultaneously available, they can be ordered either way, giving two distinct shortest supersequences. Also, since `nums` is a permutation of `[1, n]`, the unique shortest supersequence must have length exactly `n`; if the constraints only determine fewer elements, it's not unique. Walk through Example 1: edges 1→2 and 1→3 leave both 2 and 3 with in-degree 0 after 1, so orderings [1,2,3] and [1,3,2] both work → false. Example 2 has no constraint involving 3, so 3 is unconstrained → false. Example 3 gives edges 1→2, 1→3, 2→3; after removing 1 only 2 is available, then only 3 → true. Constraints (n up to 10⁴, total sequence length up to 10⁵) demand an O(n + E) graph algorithm.
k: Consecutive pairs in each sequence define directed edges; nums is the unique shortest supersequence iff the resulting DAG has a unique topological order.
A topological order is unique iff Kahn's queue always holds exactly one zero-in-degree node.
The unique order must contain all n values; otherwise some element is unconstrained and multiple supersequences exist.

a.n: Approach 1: Topological Sort (Kahn's Algorithm) with uniqueness check
a.i: Build a graph where each consecutive pair in a subsequence adds an edge. Run BFS-based topological sort; at each step there must be exactly one node with in-degree 0. If ever zero nodes remain but not all n were output, or more than one candidate exists, uniqueness fails. This directly encodes 'only one valid next choice at every position', which is precisely what makes the shortest supersequence unique.
s: For each sequence, add edge seq[j] -> seq[j+1], deduplicating edges per pair to keep in-degrees correct.
Initialize a queue with all nodes of in-degree 0.
Repeat: if queue size != 1, return false (either stuck early or ambiguous choice). Pop the single node, append to result.
For each neighbor, decrement in-degree; push when it hits 0.
Return true iff all n nodes were processed.
a.t: O(n + S) where S is the total length of all sequences — building edges and Kahn's BFS each visit every node/edge once (edge dedup via hash/set adds log-free hashing cost).
a.sp: O(n + E) for adjacency lists, in-degree array, and queue, where E ≤ S is the number of distinct edges.

a.n: Approach 2: Greedy position check against nums
a.i: Instead of running a full topological sort, verify that nums itself is forced. For each consecutive pair (a, b) in nums, check that some sequence contains a immediately followed by b; additionally, every consecutive pair within each sequence must be adjacent in nums (otherwise that sequence would force an order contradicting a shortest supersequence). If every adjacent pair of nums appears as an adjacent pair in some sequence, then each step of the reconstruction is uniquely determined, so nums is the unique shortest supersequence.
s: Record pos[v] = index of value v in nums.
Insert every consecutive pair (seq[j], seq[j+1]) into a hash set of pairs.
If any such pair is non-adjacent in nums (pos[b] != pos[a] + 1), return false — it contradicts nums being a shortest supersequence.
For each adjacent pair (nums[i], nums[i+1]), require it to exist in the pair set; otherwise the boundary is unconstrained and another supersequence exists.
Return true if all checks pass.
a.t: O(S + n) — one pass over all sequences plus one pass over nums, with O(1) hash-set lookups.
a.sp: O(S) for storing up to S distinct consecutive pairs.

w: In an interview, lead with the topological-sort framing since it generalizes to 'count number of shortest supersequences' style follow-ups; the greedy pair-check is a slick optimal alternative worth mentioning. Key pitfalls: forgetting to deduplicate duplicate edges (inflating in-degrees and breaking Kahn's), checking only queue emptiness instead of requiring size exactly 1, and assuming a valid topological order suffices without verifying length n. Edge cases: n = 1 (trivially true if 1 appears in some sequence — both solutions handle it correctly since count==1 and no pairs needed... note the greedy version returns true here regardless, which matches because a single-element permutation is always the unique shortest supersequence). Follow-ups: how many distinct shortest supersequences exist (count products of choices during Kahn's), or reconstruct one valid supersequence instead of validating nums.
